articles.title: I bought Thunderbolt 5 and got USB4 40G: re-benchmarking a two-machine llama.cpp RPC setup across three links and six models
articles.excerpt: This post is a follow-up to my previous benchmark. It tests six models across three links — 5GbE, "fake TB5," and USB 10GbE — comparing how link speed affects performance. I'd originally planned to te…
articles.body: This post is a follow-up to my previous benchmark. It tests six models across three links — 5GbE, "fake TB5," and USB 10GbE — comparing how link speed affects performance. I'd originally planned to test only TB5, then move on to other things. Buy a cable, plug it in, measure, done — a few hours, tops. But TB5 failed to establish end-to-end connectivity on the ASMedia4242 chip. I wasn't convinced at first, but eventually gave up trying. It looks like ASM870/870E can't do DMA-based end-to-end transfer unless you swap out the ASMedia4242 module itself. So I bought USB 10GBps afterward — except TB5 still doesn't support USB10GBps, so it only works over USB-C 10 (roughly 7.2Gbps measured). Manually installing Realtek and tuning the protocol turned out to be the easier path in comparison.
articles.author: faliye

articles.title: Your background job checked permissions when it was queued. Who is it acting for when it runs?
articles.excerpt: A pattern I keep running into: the API handler checks that the user can export the report, delete the project or send the invoices, then drops a job on a queue and returns 202. The worker picks it up…
articles.body: A pattern I keep running into: the API handler checks that the user can export the report, delete the project or send the invoices, then drops a job on a queue and returns 202. The worker picks it up later and does the work with a service account that can touch everything. That check happened at enqueue time. If the job sits in the queue for an hour, or retries over a day, the user could have been removed from the org, lost the admin role, or had the project moved to another workspace in the meantime. The worker never asks again, so the action still goes through. A few things that have helped on teams I've worked with: Put the acting user ID and tenant ID in the job payload, never only the object ID. A job without an actor is impossible to audit later.

articles.title: How to Optimize SQL Queries: 20 Proven Best Practices
articles.excerpt: A slow SQL query is one of the easiest ways to ruin a fast application. You can have a clean architecture, a great cache, and a powerful server - and still watch a page hang because one query scans a…
articles.body: A slow SQL query is one of the easiest ways to ruin a fast application. You can have a clean architecture, a great cache, and a powerful server - and still watch a page hang because one query scans a million rows without an index. Over the years, I have optimized hundreds of SQL queries across many production systems. Most of the wins come from the same small set of techniques, applied again and again. Some of them are obvious. Some of them go against advice you have probably heard. To make them easy to remember, I have grouped 20 proven techniques into 6 themes you can reach for whenever a query gets slow.
articles.author: Anton Martyniuk

articles.title: Your GET /docs/:id has a permission check. Does GET /docs?
articles.excerpt: Most apps I've looked at guard single-object routes fine. You fetch the document, check the user can read it, return 403 or 404 if not. The list endpoint is where things slip. A common version: the li…
articles.body: Most apps I've looked at guard single-object routes fine. You fetch the document, check the user can read it, return 403 or 404 if not. The list endpoint is where things slip. A common version: the list query filters by tenant_id and nothing else. Inside one tenant, everybody sees every row, including private drafts, HR folders, or a project they were removed from last week. Another version: the list does filter, but search, export, autocomplete, and the "recent items" widget each run their own query, and only one of them got the filter. A few things that have worked for me: Put the permission filter in one function that returns a query, and make every list-shaped endpoint call it. Search, export, and counts included. Don't load everything and then drop rows in application code.

articles.title: A search box over 56 server-rendered cards, 13,486 characters of index, and the word pilot matching none of them
articles.excerpt: cogniprep.app/games is a hub of 56 provider It now has a search box, and the interesting part is not the matching. It is The hub page is a server component. It maps the provider list into card props S…
articles.body: cogniprep.app/games is a hub of 56 provider cards. Until this week it was a static grid: if you had an email telling you to sit something called a VEA 475, you scrolled. It now has a search box, and the interesting part is not the matching. It is what had to stay on the server, what had to be shipped to the browser to make filtering work at all, and the two queries a real candidate would type that return nothing. The cards are rendered on the server and the query only reorders them The hub page is a server component. It maps the provider list into card props and hands the whole array to a client component: < ProviderDirectory providers = { PROVIDERS } /> So the first paint and the HTML a crawler receives contain every card, search box or not.

articles.title: Give your AI ops agent read access to prod, and make every write ask first
articles.excerpt: I work at Permit, and this comes from a post on our blog about governing AI ops agents, so keep the bias in mind. Nothing below depends on our product. Incident agents are getting good at pulling logs…
articles.body: I work at Permit, and this comes from a post on our blog about governing AI ops agents, so keep the bias in mind. Nothing below depends on our product. Incident agents are getting good at pulling logs, metrics and Kubernetes events together and suggesting a root cause. The post deals with what happens when the same agent can also restart a service or edit RBAC. Investigating production and changing it are separate permissions, and they should be granted separately. Group tools by what they do The post sorts operations into four tiers: T0, inspect and read: list, get, log and metric queries, config fetches. Allowed in prod for approved agent identities, with full logging. T1, diagnose and test: profiling, dry runs, diff checks, policy simulation.

articles.title: Two AI readers agreed—and both were wrong
articles.excerpt: My workflow in TransferDue extracts unit numbers, floor areas, and prices from Thai property documents. A misread digit can still look perfectly reasonable, so I added a second reading. Then two reade…
articles.body: My workflow in TransferDue extracts unit numbers, floor areas, and prices from Thai property documents. A misread digit can still look perfectly reasonable, so I added a second reading. Then two readers agreed on the same wrong answer. Gemini read the number correctly, but my code accepted the answer with the most votes. I changed the rule for accepting an answer. Across 315 checks of extracted values, wrong answers accepted without a warning fell from 57 to 35—a 38.6% reduction . Correct answers barely increased. More mistakes became visible, but more values also needed manual checking. Why asking twice wasn't enough A wrong unit number, floor area, or sale price can change how someone understands a transaction. I wanted extra checks on those values.

articles.body: Full spoilers follow for Avatar: Seven Havens Season 1, Episodes 10-13! One thing that’s abundantly clear in the final four episodes of Avatar: Seven Havens “Book 1: Survival” is that between all the mysteries, theorizing, and big plot questions – how are there two Avatars? articles.body: Spoilers follow for Nocturne Episodes 1 and 2, which are available on Apple TV now. Apple TV’s new thriller series, Nocturne, aims to draw audiences in with just the right balance of the familiar and the unexpected. The show asks what happens when a boy thought to be the victim of a serial killer returns alive, and follows the criminal mastermind as he maneuvers law enforcement during their race to save any other victims who may still be out there. Over the course of these first two episodes, viewers are left with questions — a mix of plot-driven intrigue, interest in character development, and a touch of side-eye around potential logic gaps or plot conveniences. Nocturne is based on Lars Kepler’s crime novels (The Sandman and Lazarus), and adapted by Rowan Joffe and John Hlavin for TV.
